To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
acute stress impaires working memory performance for tasks requiring maintenance and executive processing but not for those only requiring maintenance.
acute stress impeded the performance on the Ospan and the digit span backward but not on the digit span forward task in healthy young men.
cold pressor stress impaires working memory performance on the O-span task, but not on the digit span task, and that these impairments are related to stress-induced cortisol increases.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of acute stress on working memory.
the effects of stress on cognitive processes, in particular on working memory.
the effects of stress on cognitive functions and the underlying neurobiological mechanisms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
stress impairs WM tasks that demand both maintenance and executive processing but not WM tasks that demand only maintenance.
the HPA axis is involved in the regulation of the executive functions of WM but not in the maintenance of information.
stress impairs WM for tasks with a high demand on executive processing but not for tasks with a low demand on executive processing.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
acute stress impaires performance on WM tasks that require executive processing, but not on tasks that only require the maintenance of information.
stress impairs WM tasks requiring executive functions but not WM tasks that only demand maintenance.
acute stress impinges on the executive functions of the brain but not on the maintenance functions of the brain.
The main takeaway from our work is that
stress can impair WM performance for tasks that demand executive processing.
stress impairs the executive processing component of WM, which is in line with previous findings on the impact of stress on executive control.
the O-Span test is sensitive to acute stress and can be used in future research as a reliable measure of the impact of stress on executive processing.
